projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Steve A. Kallas was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Steve A. Kallas. Mr. Kallas was in the United States Army 394th Regiment, Second Battalion, 99th Division. Mr. Kallas served in the European theater and his highest rank during World War II was Staff Sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and we recorded this at Mr. Kallas' home in Stow, Ohio, on June 28th, 2001. Steve's age at the time was 78.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Well, let's see. It was March 13th, 1943. I got out on March 3, 1946, but the -- and of course the draft, which was imposed, they drafted everybody -- or supposedly everybody. But, again, in the lower socioeconomic strata, which we were in, plus being the first generation from overseas, wetbacks you might say, they're the first ones they get, and you can't tell me otherwise that these people show partiality -- or impartiality, they aren't partial. Well, anyway, so that's how I got started in '43. And, of course, you went through all of the testing and the immunization shots and so on and find out how dumb you are or whatever, which they did pretty well, I guess. So initially basic training in Camp Hood, Texas. That's not in this thing. And from there they -- your IQ test that you took confirmed whether you were an idiot or what, and in this case they sent us to school. I think it was a parking lot for people that they could grab ahold of and throw them in the infantry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Only idiots went into the infantry; is that what you're saying?

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Yeah, right. And we went to -- I went to LSU, which is in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. It was an engineering course and the engineering course was quite intensive. You didn't want to flunk out so you did as well as you could and you didn't want to flunk out anyway. But anyway, one of the last tests they did -- believe it or not, they wanted to see if you could become a doctor. If you had enough brains, they would -- and I knew guys that made it and became physicians and -- by going to the ASTP school that -- they gave us one last test and the outcome was -- of course many of us didn't make it, and I was one of them. They threw us into the 99th Infantry Division which was in Waco -- Paris, Texas. Near Paris, Texas. The 99th Division was gearing up for overseas duty and I got thrown into the E Company of 394 Regiment and -- which is part of the -- you know, whole division. Now, the makeup of a division is about anywhere from 15 to 18,000 people. You may know that, right? Do you know that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: But the guys that get, pardon the expression, the crap, are very few. They're about -- making up about 10 percent of the whole division and they get 90 percent of the casualties, which I can understand why. Well, anyway, the guys that I dealt with were supposedly some professional soldiers, right? Yeah. Well, anyway, it turned out I had to be dumb.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why's that?

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Well, also I think it comes back to my upbringing with -- you always had to do the best no matter what, you figure everybody is doing the same. Well, one of the things that we did was a shoot off to see -- the highest score would get a three-day pass to Dallas. With a BAR. A BAR was, you know -- if you know what it is, it weighs 21 pounds and all that kind of stuff. And I just shot the ass off of the thing, I mean. And the other guys either must have been laying down on the job, but I got 236 out of 250 and one other guy got 238. He was in another regiment.

So my deal was I went to Dallas with a pass, which -- I think the other guys must have been laying down on the job. But enough guys got those. It wasn't only one BAR. And a BAR weighs 21 pounds, it's got a bipod mount, and each clip has 20 rounds in it, and they weigh a pound and a half each, each clip. And you shoot the thing by bumping it to get off a shot, a burst of three. If you hold it down, it will just jump all over hell. Well, most machine guns do the same thing unless they're really anchored down. So anyway, with the BAR -- and after a while, when we got going and had enough training that they figured, okay, guys, we're ready -- yeah, right. You're ready for sudden death. Oh, shoot.

Well, anyway, the guys we had there and the very guys that I knew -- I was in the Second Platoon with John Lucy as the Platoon Sergeant and my Squad Leader was a guy by the name of Al Pacino out of Cleveland out of the Lyndhurst Flores [ph] group. Nice Italian boy. And he was my Squad Leader. Well, anyway, this is just to let you know that my memory hasn't slipped. Alzheimer's has not gotten me. So are we still bullshitting too much on this thing or what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not at all. I have plenty of tape.

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Yeah, I understand. But is this pertinent to the project here?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Everything's pertinent. If it stirs some kind of memory, yeah, that's fine. And if there's too much that doesn't pertain to the war, I just cut it out --

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Oh, okay. Well, all right. But -- and our company commander at the time was a guy by the name of McGee, Captain McGee. Now, this is important, I'll tell ya, because we also had a pertinent Colonel by the name of Wertheimer. He should have been called "Werthlessheimer." But, no, I'm not being derogatory. Well, I am being derogatory. But he -- I'll tell you the story.

Well, anyway, after we got all trained up and they figured you were good enough to go, they shipped us to Myles Standish up in Massachusetts and a couple days there and from there we went overseas. It was the stinking Liberty ship, some English rotten, old hull of a ship. They served us food down at the lowest point of the ship and it stunk. And the British don't know how to cook.

Although, I was managing director of a company and I worked in England, and we had good cooks where I stayed. They were Italian, they were French, they were something else, but they weren't English. Well, anyway, they used to let us out in the daytime to go onboard outside to see how we were faring on the ocean, you know, and I struck up a conversation with one of the sailors. He turned out to be a Greek, which I am. I don't know if you noticed that, but that's me here. And after that, I ate with the crew. I didn't eat with our guys. So I had good fare. They didn't have an English cook on there either, I don't imagine.

But, anyway, the rest of the -- a lot of guys couldn't handle the motion of the ship. I loved it. The more bouncing around, the better. Well, anyway, so we finally got over to England and spent a few days and didn't do much. I got to London once, I think, and the rest of the time was cross on the LST and we landed in Le Havre and from Le Havre we went to Aubel, Belgium in open 6-by-6 trucks. Now, this is kind of getting cold. It was late October, early October -- in October and it's cold. But in open trucks. And I being the BAR man, I had to sit on top of the truck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is in '44, right?

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Yeah, 1944. Yeah, right. So anyway, we got going and they lined us up right across the Siegfried Line. And this is now starting early November. No cover. We didn't have anything. Just a friggin' hole, you know. And our clothing was abominable. Not only that, not very warm. You had an overcoat and didn't even have a jacket, sweaters and so on, and shoes, combat boots, all leather, no insulation. Guys with nice boots had them in the back. We didn't have them. Well, anyway, late November.

We used to have patrols, we'd go out on patrol. This was just to give you something so you don't sit in a muddy hole all day. You couldn't have a fire. They built some log cabins using timber log cabins, but the boys used to like to gamble and be inside there. And I didn't want any part of that because I figured those son of a bitches will lob one in there and get you all or come in there with a party, could wipe you out.

Well, anyway, so here you are -- foxhole, starting to rain, muck and mire, and around early December now, after making patrols, just to give you some little action, Lieutenant -- our platoon Lieutenant, a guy by the name of Buford Mayberry, a good ole southern boy. I mean, he would have been a good soldier. His brother, by the way, became a Major General, he got the Congressional Medal of Honor. So this guy all the time was vying his brother. Well, his brother went in on D Day and we came in much later of course.

Well, anyway, on this one patrol he stepped on a mine and of course lost a leg, blew it up a small tree. And of course this is just before the battle started and, you know, of course he got evacuated, and I visited him here in -- he's in Sumpter, South Carolina. Well, anyway -- so a short time after that the Germans, you could see the rascals. Their bunkers, you could take a direct hit and they would bounce right off, big artillery shells and so on. And of course those guys had trenches that they could come out and do you damage if they wanted to.

But they started a -- just before the battle started they were shooting almost 24 hours a day, machine gunfire, and you could hear it hitting the trees and it was going as far back as it could go. And of course the object was to keep you down and -- Well, anyway, I guess I had to be the dumbest guy - I guess I had to be the dumbest guy, because I started shooting back at them with my BAR. Well, this Colonel Wertheimer, who always was one of these puffery guys, he went "Oh, gee. I'm the Colonel here and, boy, you guys gotta do what I tell ya or I'll kill ya." Yeah, a bunch of...

Well, anyway, here we are in the open firing the BAR, ___ , and he comes up to see what's going on. Whoop-dee-do, here he comes. He sees my BAR, he raises hell with me. He raises hell -- he gets the Captain. This time -- by this time McGee was Battalion now, he was one of his staff. Well, anyway, so he calls Captain Patterson who had become our company commander and he had him break me from a PFC to a Private. Now, what reasonable man -- which this guy wasn't, and very stupid. You know, you're out in the open, everything ___ up, you're shooting a goddamn weapon, and the guy thinks you should be spittin' polish.

Well, so anyway, I got broke from PFC to Private. Thank you very much. I needed the money. I used to send all my money home because there we were, you know. Well, anyway, so after that -- it took me about two days to clean up the BAR. I had thrown away my bipod on one of those - one of those cockamamie - cockamamie patrols we had because it would hang up and snag in the bushes and brambles and so on, so I had thrown it away. So I had to go back and find it and then it took me about two days to clean up that BAR. And of course the Captain says, "Okay. That's it. You're just a Private now." Goddamn.

Well, anyway, we used to put out patrols every night and we had an outpost duty. On this particular night, it was about the 16th -- yeah, it had to be the 16th of December or maybe the 15th, because it started on the 16th. Al Pacino and I were on outpost that night. And the reason you're there is obviously to see if you could hold back five divisions, which you no-way-in-hell could. Well, anyway, come that morning, here we are maybe 300 yards from the biggest bunker that they had. So about 5:30 the next morning, which is the 16th or the 17th, they cut loose the biggest barrage you ever saw. It was just like the 4th of July -- more so. The sky lit up. It was -- I mean, that sucker really, really created a lot of uproar, I'll tell ya. Well, anyway, it took about two hours. It was about two hours, they were blasting away. And of course what they were trying to do was knock out your stuff behind you. And all along they kept saying "Oh, there's nothing going on, boys. We're gonna have a long winter here, that's why we built these log cabins." Bull.

No General worth his -- none of these Generals were around; they all took off. They were in Paris, London, everywhere else. Library of Congress, these guys should have been prosecuted. I mean, they abandoned their duty. No, they did it. They just wanted a battle of attrition, that's all it was, to wear them down, wear us down. Well, anyway, after the barrage stopped two hours later, about 5:30 in the morning started -- 5:30, 6:30, 7:30 or so it quieted down and ole Al Pacino and myself said let's get the hell back here to the company. Now, here you are in a spit of protection and the rest of it is way over here. I'm with the BAR and ole Al was with a rifle, you know, he was... So we waited a little bit and we started running across that opening and I can't imagine how -- maybe 3, 4, 500 yards.

They saw us running and of course they unloaded again some 88s on us and ole Al hit a slit trench in front of me and he was in first. Now, this sounds like a lot of bullshit, but he hit the ground into the slit trench and I was on top of him and I was listening to what he was doing. He was shaking like a dog shitting razor blades, and I said, "Hey, Al, I'm on top." So, anyway, we got up and I remember looking around and there was some hellish big shells laying around that didn't cut loose, you know. So then -- I'm really embellishing this thing, you won't find that in there. Nah, I'm not embellishing. I got tired of writing that son of bitchin' thing. Pardon me for -- I'm really getting cranked up here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've heard much worse.

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: I don't mean that. I mean I'm really getting cranked up here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's alright.

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: So we got back to the company and the trees were just flattened. There was only one guy killed, a guy by the name of -- he was an Indian yet, a real American Indian. A guy by the name -- I don't know what his name was. We used to call him the Chief, and he was in with a guy by the name of Larson. And something got him in the hole, it could have been shrapnel or something, and ole Larson came out and he went nuts. He went -- they had to, you know, escort him back. You know, he was really out of it.

Well, anyway, the word came down that we were supposed to retreat. Word came down. Take only your weapons. Don't take anything else, which was a mistake. Around 11:00 o'clock they all started leaving. However, they told me, the BAR guy -- I was told to stay back, give the company a half an hour start. Now, it sounds incredulous. Now, these guys were somewhat militarily trained, right?

No. One BAR guy to hold off -- and there were five divisions coming through, all those Panzer divisions and who the hell else they were, I didn't know -- we weren't formally introduced or anything like that, you know. Well, anyway, they all left -- left me behind and all they wanted was a half an hour start and they went. Now, where the hell did they go? I waited. I walked up and down. I wasn't pulling sentry duty or anything like that. I wanted to see what was in some of these holes.

And sure enough, some lowdown son of a bitch, they had a bunch of D bars in their hole, and I took those D bars, of course, I wanted to eat them. You know what they are? Hard candy that was really designed for the South Pacific so it wouldn't melt, you know. But it produces high energy, gives you a sugar fit or something like that. But anyway, that's all I had to eat for the next three days, and luckily I found them.

Well, anyway, I walked back -- and I'll recall this until my dying day -- there was an old fence, a farm fence, I put my BAR on that, rested it there, and I was waiting for those buggers to come in. Now, they were using a little psychology, which we never did. You could hear them yelling and screaming and they had dogs with them. Now, my half an hour was up and these guys were getting close and I wasn't about to stir up a mess by shooting a bunch of 'em so I took off. I gave them a half an hour. It took me all day to catch up with them.

Now, you see where they were? They were hell and gone. As I started back, you saw trucks turned over, artillery pieces -- they should have spiked the artillery pieces so they couldn't be used. And in one of the trucks I found a blanket, which I should have taken my own before, but I put it around my neck, and a bottle booze. This had to be an officer's truck because these buggers got liquor rations, which they should never have. They shouldn't give them liquor. You need a clear head. You don't need a stupid head. You know, and these guys ... okay, guys. Meatheads.

Well, anyway, that was my first drink of booze. I was about 22 years old then. Now, that's a rarity in this day and age. I kept going and I finally caught up with the same Colonel, Colonel Wertheimer, who was supposed to be a hard-nuts case and so on, you know, a tough man. Bull. Here he was with McGee and a couple other guys and he was kind of on a mound, all of the sycophants were around him, there's the chief and the chief didn't know what to do. He's smoking, walking around like a stupe. He wanted to surrender.

Yeah. McGee says, "The fuck we are. The hell we are. We're leaving." Now, you can imagine how far this was back, now, this is way back there. Subsequent to this time -- and I found out later from communicating with some other guys, you know, the last four, five years -- they had to drag him out of some cave. He found a cave. He didn't want to go anywhere else. They dragged him out and got him back and they reduced his rank. They should have shot the son of a bitch.

But, anyway, here's old tough nuts Wertheimer, get that number. No, you hate those kind of guys that embarrass and so on, they're so tough and make your life miserable and reduce me from PFC to Private. Well, anyway, I remember this, too. You didn't have water. You know, we never had supplies. You never got rations. Believe it not, it sounds like bullshit, but it's not. You talk to some of the guys who were with me that survived, they'd tell you the same dang story. Well, anyway, so we kept going.

I finally caught up with the company and it was starting to get dark, it was about the 17th, 18th of December, and it was starting to snow, the visibility was down to zero, and now here's where the captured guns get involved. They start shooting -- you can tell the difference between your weapons and their weapons, ours had a different cyclic rate. Theirs is higher. Well, anyway, some of that occurred. So you don't know are they friendly or foes or whatever and you don't know where the hell you're going. So, again, I caught up with the company and we were retreating to somewhere, I didn't know where.

Whoever was at the head of the line -- and we had to hang onto the guy's coat that was in front of you. It was so damn dark. Now, the American artillery was trying to hit guys over us and the Germans were trying to hit us. We were going down through a - through a -- like the valley of the -- not the valley of death, but the charge of the 600 going down in the valley and we were going down in the valley.

Now, these leather shoes are worthless. I mean, you can't - you can't maneuver, you can't run. You slip. You take two steps and you're slipping all over; it's like a cartoon. Well, anyway, there was guys hit and the orders came you don't bring anybody with you, you leave them there. The thinking is that the Germans would pick them up or take them as prisoners. Some of that happened, but a lot of that happened like this: A bullet between the eyes, you're really down. They didn't want to care for you either. And they were the SS Panzer coming through and they were notorious for not being very nice people.

Well, anyway, we were going down and it was mucky, and I recall going down this incline and down at the bottom was a stream and that stream was running pretty good and a lot of guys got across, and they weren't as heavily burdened as I was. I had this blanket around my neck. I had the clips of -- BAR clips and the BAR and I jumped -- tried to jump the creek and I landed in the middle of the son of a bitch. Oh, I got climbing out of that thing madder than hell. But I was more mad at my stupidity than the problem. I just had too much load on me. If I didn't have all of that -- plus you carry your raincoat, that's the other thing you had, a raincoat and an entrenching tool. And I got out on the other side, took all my clothes off, wrung them out. Now, this is December 18th. Cold, cold. And I wrung out my -- of course there was instructions on the bottom of your boot that said, "Pour this out."

So I poured the -- no, I'm kidding you about that -- poured the water out of my boots, took my pants, my underwear off, wrung them off. Now, this is about -- well, it's after -- you know, it's dark. I put them back on. Colder than a son of a bitch. Kept on going. You didn't know where the hell you were going. Well, anyway, as I was going -- and I recall this very vividly -- there was somebody that didn't want to continue on lying there, he must have been wounded, he says, "Hey, how about that blanket?" and I gave him the blanket. Now, what a nice guy I was. That son of a bitch.

Well, anyway, I gave it to him. We reached a barn. There was a huge barn we got into, and I don't know why I was still standing. I spent the rest of the night there, which wasn't much of the rest of the night and -- shivering and shaking. There was no straw in the place so you couldn't get into straw. I was lying on the ground and it was cold and my body must have been pretty good functioning, but it shook all night. The next morning we got up and got out. We had made the Second Division, that's who we finally caught up with, and -- they gathered up what guys they could gather up and out of the 394th there was about 200 guys. Where the hell are the rest of them? You know, they're either wounded, dead, or something like that.

Now, they said, "Hey, guys. We gotta go over there and take positions in a place called Elsenborn, former German artillery range." Isn't that nice? And anybody that felt he couldn't make it because of the severity of our previous 48 hours or whatever, drop out. One guy dropped out; it was a goddamn Lieutenant. So the rest of us kept going. And, again, they usually picked officers, I think, on age. Well, because they figured they're a little more experienced maybe. But no guts. No guts. And we were dumb.

So anyway, the only thing they could give us was quarter sticks of dynamite -- the ground was frozen -- and some sandbags, no sand in them, of course, to take with you to fill as you dig a hole so you could have some protection around your hole, and I used those bags to protect my feet. I put them on my feet because my feet were cold. And you used the quarter-inch sticks of dynamite to just start the hole, and I had my entrenching tool. I didn't leave anything behind, if I could help it. Well, another guy and ourselves, we dug a hole and it took us days. We were digging holes all the time. And all you had to cover your hole was either your raincoat or the other guy's raincoat or if you had a shelter or a poncho like, which would be a little bigger, to cover the hole. And of course it was snowing like crazy. And so there we were -- it took us days or what seemed like days in this friggin' hole to dig it, because it was so dadgum hard and all you have is an entrenching tool, I'm sure you know what those are. I've got mine in the garage. I do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You still have it?

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, that's the only thing I have. So every night we'd have to go out on patrol and I would have to go out more than anybody else. Now, the clothing you had was miserable clothing. Your boots -- you didn't dare take your shoes off, because if you did, your feet would swell, couldn't get your boots back on. We would get -- occasionally we'd get stockings. So you took your dirty stockings off, which weren't dirty, you put the clean ones on and put your shoes back on, because you couldn't get them back on. And all the clothing we had was a -- starting from the inside: woolen underwear; pants and top, and the pants had -- the drawers had a slit in them so you could take a bowel movement if you had to; a shirt, wool shirt; a sweater, an M -- no, you didn't -- yeah, you had an M43 jacket which was a wool-lined jacket. We didn't have any of those fancy, you know, insulated jackets because they were afraid if you had a gut wound or something, the stuff would blow in and contaminate the wound. So that's all you had, believe it or not.

Once in a while they'd give us clean clothes, which we would put on, and I would put the clean clothes on and put the old clothes on top. I looked like a mushroom after awhile. Well, anyway, we used to go out on patrol every night. Our gloves consisted of a leather-palmed glove and it was just fabric on the outside. Not worthy of the name glove. Well, anyway, so we'd have to go -- I would have to go out every night, every night. Now, there's other guys here, guys. Get some of the other guys. No. Well, anyway, I didn't have to shoot anybody, luckily, stir up a hornet's nest on the other side. I think they were all in their holes, too, and you couldn't -- they always had the best positions.

We had the wide-open, wide-open places. And of course after a three- or four-hour trip in snow, you're lucky to find your hole because it gets covered with snow. Not only that, you're lucky our own guys don't shoot you as you come in, see, and that's what happened. Well, anyway, in the morning they would try to blast us out of our holes with 88s and you're sitting in your hole and you're saying, "Oh son of a bitch, it's getting close." And they would thump in maybe a half dozen of 'em. You know, scatter them all over. And luckily the snow, of course, covers you up pretty good so they never got you.

The worst part also was at night you didn't dare get out of your hole because somebody's gonna shoot you, your own guys. I mean, after all of the goings on. And of course if you had to relieve yourself, at least take a pee, you'd use your steel helmet. Not your helmet liner; your helmet. And if you had to have a bowel movement -- I would get out of my hole, take your clothes off or lower your trousers, you're sitting out there like a duck. You're sitting -- you've got to relieve yourself. Some guys - some guys never got out of their holes, they were so afraid. And some guys wouldn't get out of the hole. Other guys would threaten them with throwing a grenade down their hole. "If you don't get out of that hole, boy, here comes a grenade for ya."

Oh, well, anyway, this went on from late December -- we had a truce around Christmastime, that was the only hot meal we got. One guy at a time could go back to the chow wagon, which was way back there, too, to get you some chow and then you'd come back to your hole and eat it. And that was the only truce. And of course the cooks never wanted to come up near you anyway. All we ever got was some K rations, that's K rations, three meals a day. You know, breakfast, lunch, supper. And after a while you couldn't eat the stuff, it was so goddamn terrible. And not K rations -- there was K rations. It wasn't C rations. It wasn't hot rations. And we were starting to look black. In the hole, we would get some soil and get some gasoline, we'd go way back somewhere and get some gas and put it in the ground -- in the pile of dirt and ignite it or melt the rations, the boxes, heat your coffee, and then after a while all that soot made you look like you were black. The only thing showing was your teeth.

And that's the only thing I ever did in the way of sanitation is brush your teeth. You couldn't shave. You didn't want to shave. You couldn't anyway. They didn't care if you did or didn't because you're not gonna last long. They didn't care. Well, anyway, this is now -- all of January we're there and then early February we were starting to do some movement and about that time they sent some guys back to Malmedy for a wash-up and get cleaned up and so on, and I was kind of unhappy that I didn't go.

It turns out the guys that did go got executed by the SS troops that came through there, they hadn't secured it completely and killed those fellas summarily, just put them out there. Some of our guys. So I was -- I had to be the luckiest devil around. Lucky was my middle name, I'll tell ya. So anyway, what they had us do is chop trees to give us exercise. Instead of giving us a nice trip to Paris or something, no, all the officers went there. I know you're getting bored here. Sorry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, not at all.

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: No, I'll hurry it up here if I can. We were chopping trees, cutting them down and then cutting them up in eight-foot lengths so you make a corduroy road for the trucks and tanks and whatever. The tanks really couldn't move unless the ground was hard around roads. Well, anyway, that was ours. Then finally I got sent back to a place called Eupen in Belgium -- I think Holland, Belgium, one of the two Belgium -- and got cleaned up, a bunch of guys went together, and when I started peeling off my clothes, they couldn't believe that skinny runt, that was me. They thought I was a huge fellow.

Well, anyway, so that was the reason. Got us cleaned up. All we got was a doughnut and then back to the ole grind. So anyway, after that -- let's see. Now it's starting - starting late February, early March. The weather was getting better and we started moving and of course the Air Force was getting active because the weather was better. We used to see them as they left our lines, that ack-ack would come up and, man, once in a while they'd get some, but it was - it was ferocious the way those -- you could probably almost walk on that ack-ack that they were throwing up. The 88 was a good gun and we had something -- the 90s -- ours were 90s and those were pretty good, but they weren't helping us at all.

Well, anyway, prior to that -- or backing up a little bit, I recall standing -- I would get out of my hole and walk around like a moron or something. No, you had to do something. And I would go and visit other guys, and I remember this fellow -- a guy by the name of Tuttle [ph], which I didn't mention in there either. We were standing on top of the hole and here comes a lone plane strafing us. Two guys come down to strafe us. Now, he went in head first into the hole and I went in feet first. I didn't think it was a good idea to go -- feet first is good. Well, anyway, he went down feet first, landed on his haunches, and I landed on the back of his leg here. He twisted his leg and he let out a scream like I thought -- I said, "What the heck happened? You got hurt? You got shot?" "No. You broke my leg." So he got out of there. The guy's name is Tuttle. So he should have thanked me. I'm sure he did after a while.

Well, anyway, one lone plane comes -- and it could have been - it could have been an American one, for all we know, because they're dumb enough to -- if they see something out there... Well, anyway, so where the hell am I? We got moving and we were starting toward the Rhine, but we had to go into a place, the Ruhr Pocket, which was - which was, you know, the area of Germany which produced all sorts of things, armaments and so on, a highly industrialized area, and we had to go there and then everything was just -- how it evolved after that, it's kind of hard to export -- expart [sic] -- tell you how it went.

But, anyway, it was evolving into house-to-house combat in which you had to, of course, search for soldiers. You didn't dare take chances and they were always -- they were waiting for you. Well, anyway, the -- that's how that whole thing got started. But about that time the elements of the Ninth Division captured the Remagen Bridge. And we were way up there to assault the rocket launching area, the Peenemunde rocket launching area and we were almost there, you could see at night the rockets taking off for England.

Once in a while they would fail to go to its target which would be, again, England or even some rural areas. They would run out of gas and come down. But the -- we were going for the big stuff, the V-2s, which was at Peenemunde and, as I said, we could see the rockets taking off at night.

We hadn't quite reached it when the elements of the Ninth Division captured the bridge, the Remagen Bridge, and we were the ones closest to the bridge. They hauled us on 6-by-6 trucks, they packed us like sardines, lights blazing. This is wartime now. Lights blazing and we were going like hell down toward wherever the bridge was and we only had one medic and the medic was sitting on the tailgate of the -- there must have been about 50 guys with their equipment on one 6-by-6 truck.

But, I mean, it was a convoy. And ole Moore, the guy's name was Moore, he was sitting on the end like -- and his foot in the bale. You know how the bales are, the big truck bales? You lower the gate, and his foot was in there, and a plane came over strafing the convoy. And when that happens, it's every man for himself, I'll tell ya, and we shot out of the back end of that truck and that poor devil wasn't moving fast enough. His foot was still in the bale. We just knocked him over, knocked him over, and he was hanging - he was hanging from that bale on his foot. And of course -- the truck is up pretty high and you have to jump and we must have jumped off of those things like a bunch of rabbits or deers or whatever you want to call us. You make a ditch, and we were waiting for another plane to come over so we could scatter some more. Luckily it didn't.

Only one guy, other than this guy, got hurt and it was - it was the chaplain. He was sitting in some truck in the middle between the truck driver and somebody else, he's the only one that got it. That goes to show you we were the nice guys. That's no bullshit either. That guy -- that has to tell you something. I don't know what it'll tell you. Then we got on the truck and we got into town there, Remagen, whatever its name is. This side of the bridge is called something and on the other side something else, but we called it the Remagen Bridge.

And we got into that town, it must have been 2:00 o'clock in the morning and of course dark, and the Germans were shelling that bridge and they were trying to knock it down with everything that they had. Small arms fire and artillery. And it turned out that they had women spotters on our side of the bridge trying to spot for the German artillery and somehow we found them. Not me, but somebody found them. And the story goes that they shot them, which is what they deserve. You're a combatant. But, again, you're a civilian.

But anyway, we got orders to go across the bridge, because we were the full division there and it was only a small group that made contact. And 2:00 o'clock in the morning, dark, shelling to beat hell. And who do you think they selected to send across first? Me. The guy in front of me was the scout at that time, a guy by the name of Samuelson out of Washington state. I never saw him again. But anyway, here we were. Now, it's dark and all you can see is a little bit of light from bursts of flares and so on and as we started across -- and as I recall, we were running a wide beam. You couldn't step off anywhere because they had holes in them and so on.

And as we started across, he was in front of me and the rest of the company was behind me, a shell burst happens and instinct takes over, the guy drops down and grabs that beam and here we are -- you know, the longer you stay there, the worst your conditions are. And the company behind me, and I didn't dare go around them, I couldn't, so I told them -- and this sounds fantastic. Now, here I am some young squirt -- he was a young guy, too. I said, "You get your ass off of here or I'm gonna kick this son of a bitch off this bridge." I would have kicked his ass off, either picked him up or thrown him, believe it or not, I do. But I don't think he ever forgave me for that one. But he got up and we kept on going.

It took us the rest of the night to get across that little ole bridge. When we got across on the other side of the bridge it was starting daylight and there was body parts all over that goddamn bridge and the other side of the bridge was some kind of a high tower-like that was part of the - part of the structures on the other side. And like I say, body parts all over. One of our tankers made it across, however the hell he got across, and he was one of the guys I trained with when I was in the early training stages at Fort Hood, a guy by the name of Jurasik [ph] out of Cleveland. He pops his head up and he says, "Hey, Steve, what the for Christ sake are you doing here?" And here I'm -- he's riding and he gave me the horse laugh. I'm walking. Okay. Well, that's alright. You guys are alright.

So anyway, we finally got out onto some high ground and we were protecting the rest of the bridge from attack from the other side, which every once in a while they'd try to do something. They were swimming frogmen down the bridge trying to blow it up, they were strafing it, they were shelling it, and everything else in between. And of course we made the other side safely. And the bridge finally collapsed, of course, and the thing that -- they had built a pontoon bridge alongside of it so when it collapsed, they still had the means to get across the bridge. So from there it was almost a walk every day that we were starting in the area that -- you had to go town to town.

We would -- we'd go into a town and the son of a bitches would be either waiting for you as a welcoming committee -- if the -- if you saw the civilians leaving waving flags or whatever, we let them go. You knew that those other guys were there and they would be the welcoming committee and every once and a while they'd shoot your ass off. And invariably as you got into approaching a town, you'd be in an open area and the open areas, which is a bad spot for you, because you have no cover, and they would, you know, start either small arms fire, machine gunfire followed up with mortars, artillery. Luckily some of those artillery shells that they had - they had -- must have used slave labor or whatever, those shells wouldn't explode. But here you have one hitting over here or hitting over here and the sucker doesn't blow up, you say to yourself... Now, the other thing is if you're staying there, you're in trouble even more. So you've got to get up and go.

Some guys wouldn't go because they just didn't want to take the chance or whatever. And if you're ever being shot at by automatic fire, you better move and you've got to pick up your feet and get going. About that time we had enough guys get killed or wounded, died by attrition, not certainly by brains, I became Squad Leader, Staff Sergeant so that -- the Colonel wasn't around anyway, so we didn't have to worry about him. I became Squad Leader and the guy that I gave the BAR to was a guy by the name of James Radery [ph] out of Habersham, Alabama. I never could find -- I went through the Internet trying to find him. I couldn't find him. Because, again, these are verifiable stories and names.

If you read this thing, you have names that we're not just concocting. I want to make that point because, you know, I've not read any of these books, Ambrose's books, Citizen Soldier. I don't want to hear that. I don't want to watch the goddamn stuff on TV. So you might say my brain is virgin from the standpoint it doesn't have too much in it. So anyway, ole Radery now became the BAR man and when we had to go into town house to house, it was a son of a bitch because there again -- I don't know what was possessing me to do these things -- I would lead the charge.

I would go to a house, we would position the guys on -- I would position the guys on the outside, and about that time you had only about six or eight guys. The squad usually is 11 to 12 guys, Squad Leader, Assistant Squad Leader, and 10 other guys. So you've got 12 guys. You're down to six, that's it, and we were moving with six. You'd get guys in there in the morning, gone at night, you don't see them again. You don't know who they are. And the guys that you did know are gone and I was still alive. Well, anyway, I would go to the door -- I could kick a door down like a mule. I kicked the friggin' door down. And then you'd have to search the house.

The guys outside would have to watch for snipers. You'd go through the whole house. You'd go to the basement. Not into the basement, because that's a bad spot, you're in a blind spot. I would yell at them in German "Come on out. Surrender. No shooting." I picked up enough German I could say that. "No shooting." If I got no response, I'd throw about four grenades down there and let 'em have it and leave.

So that was the modus operandi, you know, how to do it. So there were times -- we were always in a disadvantaged position because you're meeting something you don't know. But at night we'd always-- even in the daytime things got a little -- we'd dig a hole. You'd dig a hole or a slit trench just to get below, you know, gunfire. At night we'd go into a town, clean it out, either bang 'em good or you take over a house. We would -- I would go in and tell them "Give me a clock. Five minuten out. Rousemen [ph]," everything out, and we would take over the house and stay there at night.

Sleep in your combat boots in their bed, feather ticks and all. Never take your shoes off, you didn't dare. Not because your feet -- well, your feet would probably swell, too. But you didn't want to be caught with your pants down looking for your shoes. So that's the way it went. We would eat all their food, drink their booze, if they had any Schnapps or hard cider, which they normally did. They could have poisoned the food. They could have pissed in the booze and all that stuff, we didn't know.

I never was a drinker and never drank before, you know. But anyway, you had to have something, because we didn't get rations. Believe it or not, we didn't get rations. Those sons of a bitchin', goddamn Generals, Colonels, the whole bunch of 'em, they didn't care. You got nothing. The only thing you ever got was ammunition and you got - you got grenades. Grenades and ammunition. Once in a while you might get a K ration. Believe it or not, the son of a bitches, they ought to kill those fuckers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They had a limited ability to supply you or what?

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: No, they didn't have limited -- they never wanted to come up near you, you know. But anyway, we were like Sherman's Army, we were living off the land. So I guess maybe they figured that too, that we would eat the eggs or potatoes and that's about it. Those poor people didn't have anything either, but we ate it anyway because we were the boss in those times.

But anyway, talk about being abused. You know, I was thinking back, the way we were in that cold weather in December, January, and February, if you treated your dog as bad as we were treated, they'd knock on your door and want to haul your ass off to jail. Yeah. Well, anyway, so where were we? Anyway, that's the way house-to-house went.

And we would - we would run into some terrible situations. I remember one very vividly, that we were going into this town and there again, I was -- we would go into the street or on the street, squad -- one squad on either side of the road and a spare behind, a reserve behind you. And as we'd start down the road, you'd have to search all the houses. In this particular house that I had, I went to the door and it must have been a door -- a solid oak door, I couldn't kick that thing down. So I got ole Hague -- he's in there -- ole Melvin Hague out of Worcester, Mass or somewhere up there. We used to have a grenade -- he had a grenade launcher attachment to his rifle and you put a grenade on it. Now, it's a -- you know, it's a form charge and the thing that propels it is a shotgun shell. No shot, but just the shotgun shell itself. Well, we blasted that door down. I mean, there was nothing left of it.

And I raced into the house, searched upstairs, downstairs, threw grenades in the basement after -- and it must have taken maybe less than a minute, two minutes, at most, and I got back out on the street. Now, the street -- these devils were waiting for us -- had barbed wire so you couldn't get off the street. And the reserve squad took my position because they were on my side and they started ahead of it and I stayed behind and we started down the road and again being channeled by barbed wire. They made a right turn, almost a 90-degree turn, and the tank was sitting there. And of course the guys that were there got shot.

Now, their buddies did them a favor; they dragged them into some house. The rest of the guys took off like ruptured ducks. They took off. And then all we had was a mortar platoon or a mortar squad and we were lobbing white phosphorus into the town trying to burn the buildings around the tank, because that's the only way you can get around it, he's right there between two houses. We stayed in that town that night. We possessed a house, set up some perimeter defense, and while we were going up into that town earlier in the day, this guy -- there was a guy by the name of, believe it or not, by the name of Nixon.

Yeah. I don't know whatever happened to him either. But as we were on the road and they were shooting at us, this guy almost went horizontal from here over that barbed wire fence to the other side and we got into the house. Now, it's kind of hard to believe that this guy could do that, but he did. So we got into that house and we stayed there that night. Now, about the middle of the night, there again chicken shit Lieutenant calls for my presence in the house that he was in. He wanted me to get a couple guys and go and find these guys that were wounded and bring them back.

Now, we were burning the town and -- now, this is midnight, dark as a son of a bitch, a cobblestone road. I took two other guys; Hague was one of them. I don't know who the other guy was. He says, "Get some blankets and see if you can find those guys and bring 'em back."
[telephone rings]

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Excuse me. May I turn that off?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: But anyway, we were -- I get a call from the Lieutenant to go over there and see him and his message was "Go out there and get those guys. Oh yeah, by the way, we'll give you some medals." Thank you, you -- while he's sitting on his backside. Now, whoever dragged those fellas into those houses knew where they were. I didn't know where they were. It was midnight and later and dark. So I, again, went. Cobblestone road, every step is clump, clump. You can't even keep it quiet. So we started into town.

We got into town very vividly remembering this house and about that time you hear a gun cranking up. Uh-oh, this doesn't sound good. Here we are, middle of the road, can't see where we are. We know we're somewhere. We all squat down - squat down as low as we could get. We held a little conference. "Hey guys, what do you think?" We said, "Fuck 'em, we'll get 'em in the morning." Now, that's a helluva no. But the son of bitches that pulled them in there should have been with us, you know, because the irony of it is the next morning we're still burning the town, the tank left, and who were these buggers who would have shot our ass off in nothing flat, you know, and if I wasn't -- so we -- I guess maybe you say you're being chicken now, right? Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get your medals?

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Hell, no, we didn't get any medals. No, didn't find the guys. Well, the next morning we started back in again. Here I was first again. White phosphorus has a tendency to burn, as you know, and we were still burning the town and we continued on, stopped at the same house we stopped in the night before and I went in. You could smell burning flesh. I mean, stinks like hell. And here was this guy, he had been shot several times, his flesh was all burned off of him. His -- all you saw was a skull with the smile of death.

Somebody had done him in with his own Pick-Matic. A Pick-Matic is a little entrenching tool; it looks like a big pic, only small. It caved his skull in. And believe it or not, he had a hard-on, an erection, his penis was erected. Now, if that's -- that part of his flesh hadn't burned all off, but his upper body was burned.

Now, that's something I remember -- years later I remember going, man, I should have - I should have done something better for that guy. He had come in the morning; he was gone that night. And in many cases, that's the way it went. But anyway, from there all we did was took his dog tags off, handed them to the Lieutenant, and said, "Here you go, boy." Those miserable devils. But there were many instances like that that you wish you could have done better, but, hey, you can only do so much. You can't take a wounded. We weren't -- you can't run with a wounded person. Forget about the TV. You leave 'em behind.

If you get shot -- there had been times we were going to assault a place. You're out in the open. The first thing that they do is unload small arms on you. The first thing you do is hit the ground to try to see where you are. You know where you are, but you also want to see where you've gotta go. And I remember this: Here you are laying out in the open. There's a ridge up ahead that you can get up under, because they can't get you under that, and the machine gunfire was coming alongside my body here. So if you stay there, you're gonna get more of it. So of course you get up and run. I got up to that ridge, another guy over here was shot between the eyes, and here we were there and pretty soon you could hear these big -- they're great, big five-inch rockets, big mortars. The thing stands about four and a half, five feet high. Are you familiar with it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: Oh, I thought maybe you were shaking your head saying yeah. And a lot of times --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What fired that?

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: It's like a - it's like a mortar. It's a mortar, but it's about a five-inch mortar. Now, we could hear when they would drop them into the tube, you go bloomp, and the thing would take off. And they were trying to get us around that ridge. And then you've got a bunch of guys that got bumped off. The rest of our guys are gone. I mean, we had a bunch of runners, I'll tell ya, they didn't want to go forward. They went the other way. And when you're out by yourself -- I ran back, too. I'm not gonna stay there. What is the mission?

And in the meantime you'd hear this rocket, bloomp, and you'd count, how much longer is it gonna be before it gets you? You stop because they're trying to anticipate you running and pretty soon they can. The most -- the greatest distance is at 45 degrees, you know, down. Going up, it would be like this. So they were doing a lot of that and trying to get it out as far as they could.

But then we had guys shot there. I've seen little German kids dressed up in those uniforms -- dressed in uniforms. Pretty little kids. Shot. Not by us. I don't know who shot 'em. The kid was laying there. I remember just seeing that kid -- ah, man. You say to yourself, "Oh, wow. What in the hell is this kid doing out here?" But that happened. Other times you would see -- when we would go into these houses, I mean the little -- I remember when we'd search houses, we would search the house after we removed the occupants. I remember seeing photographs of piles of dead people. This was before we knew that these people were in these concentration camps. They never told us anything. We were too stupid to comprehend, I guess. And I looked through those pictures, there was a bunch of 'em. Piles of people dead; no clothes on. I said, "What the for Christ sakes goin' on here?" And later on, of course, we knew what was happening.

And these people, you know, want to act like "We didn't know anything about it." Baloney. Well, anyway, after these incidences we got across the Rhine of course and this was later on. We got past Munich. We got past Nuremberg - Nuremberg, yeah, Munich, Wurzburg. And in Wurzburg the town was flattened. So was Munich, flattened. But one of the things that they had were underground cellars and those underground cellars in Wurzburg were full of cognac, wines, and Champaigns and so on. And I remember a bunch of us guys got into there and we were popping corks to see how far a cork could go. We should have - we should have shot that place up just for the hell of it. But, no, no, we didn't do that. But that's all that was left of Wurzburg and Munich was devastated.

And then as the war was cranking down -- and there again, we were operating on very small, small units. The company was down to maybe 80 men instead of 180 and we'd get people and go and all that stuff, and I remember we would -- this one particular time we were, believe it or not -- again, there I was with the BAR guy, this guy Radery, and at the end of the day you'd always dig a hole, dig a slit trench, just to get out below grade. And the next morning -- this time we had some rations because we were nowhere near anything. We got a ration.

Oh, wonderful. I'm usually somewhat gregarious in the morning because I'm -- usually I feel better in the morning than I do at night. I didn't say anything and ole Radery says, "Hey, Steve. I had a dream that you were gonna get shot today." I said, "Funny thing. I dreamt the same thing." Two guys, we're not lovers, you know, you had to sleep in a hole with a guy. You'd prefer a woman, but they couldn't - they couldn't -- women in the military, forget it.

Well, anyway, as we started on that day -- and his warning was to take, you know -- and of course I dreamt the same thing. We started towards some town, which I didn't know where it was. We were on the edges of the company, Radery and I, and we were starting down in kind of a hilly terrain and down here was a German soldier and he had a box and over his shoulder he had a bird gun. Now, that guy was sweating bullets, I'll tell ya, because Radery wanted to shoot him. I said, "No, don't shoot him. We've shot enough. Don't shoot him." He said, "Let me shoot him." "No, don't shoot him." So I finally convinced the guy -- I told this guy, "No." I held up my weapon, I says, "Come on up. We're not gonna shoot you." So he came up bringing his box and his box had some rations in it, some PX rations for his troops. Where were the troops? I don't know.

Well, anyway, we used him to carry some of our weaponry, mortars and ammunition, and he had a watch on. All these guys had watches. We didn't -- we had a watch we'd pass back and forth when we were sleeping in a hole. We were one hour on/one hour off. Now, how much sleep you get on that, yeah? Well, anyway, he had a watch and I was gonna take it. The guy said his mother -- his "mutter" gave it to him. I said, "Okay. Keep it." The watch can be used as a compass, you know. Do you know that, a watch can be used as a compass? Well, so I said, "Okay. Keep it anyway." He didn't get very far and our guys took it from him saying "I had lost the watch." We could have had watches. Some guys couldn't carry a cleaning rod.

You're so tired. You walk miles, you dig holes, you're running, you're hiding, you're doing all kind of things, and you're goddamned tired you wouldn't believe. And after a while you say "I don't give a goddamn what happens. I don't care." And that's what happened with a lot of guys. Ole Wadsworth was one of those patrols we had early on that -- he and I were together. This is a guy by the name of Wadsworth out of -- he was a Mormon yet. This is -- I'm digressing here, not keeping the thing in order here. We had to go on a patrol and the snow was deep -- and this is all the time we were in this Elsenborn area. Snow up to your ass. And we had to go and just do some harassing and we had -- he was a BAR guy. We had the ammo bearer, first scout, which was Wadsworth, we had a machine gunner in the back, and a mortar and a radio communication guy and a Lieutenant, and snow up to your ass.

You're in brown clothing. Man, what a target. Beautiful. I mean, these Generals, don't they have any goddamned brains? They don't have brains. They have -- brass is all they've got. Well, anyway, ole Wadsworth and I started ahead and he-- there was a foxhole there that he walked into. There was some candy there, we took it and he and I shared it. He was in the ASTP with me in Louisiana State, so I knew the guy. And we were commiserating about the situation and saying to ourselves "This is a dog. I mean, this is bad."

And here he was, he was ahead of me, and about that time you're out there in the open again, you can't maneuver because you're wading in snow. Wading in it, not just walking on top of it -- and in brown khakis. So anyway, the Germans opened up on us and the first thing -- and ole Wadsworth, I knew he was - he was doomed because he says, "I'm tired of this," using all kind of expletives that you don't want to hear on this thing, right? Well, anyway, the first guy that got it, he got it. And they were shooting at me pretty good and here we are -- I was on a ridge and my ammo bearer was on my right side behind me, a guy by the name of Gobling [ph]. All I know is his surname, Gobling. And I was on this ridge, I just rolled down into a gully, and I kept telling this guy "Come on with me. You're in a bad spot." Well, he wouldn't move. He got shot.

I was down here. The gun jammed. And you can't see -- the Germans had smokeless powder. We had black powder. You take a shot and that thing -- it's like throwing a flamethrower out there. Well, anyway, I went back. The machine gunner's gun jammed. The mortar - the mortar people, they had a mortar or two that didn't have a firing pin in it so you can't shoot the mortars. So the whole friggin' thing went to pieces. So we pulled back. They start shelling us. We pulled back some more. We were shelling them. And here I was with the -- in the back trying to clean my BAR and then I saw this guy lying facedown over here. So it was one of our guys, obviously.

So I went over there and the guy was dead. I took his helmet and his rifle and stabbed it in the ground, put a helmet over it. About that time some idiot -- one of our idiots starts shooting at me and I could see that sucker lying down, prone position aiming, firing and one came by me like this. I just went like that. And, man, why he didn't plug me? He was just a poor shot. So we finally ended up the day -- I mean, that was a total loss. Well, getting back to this other thing when we were finding this German fellow with his box. We ate. We started ahead again and later in the day it started raining. You put on your raincoat and on the bottom of my raincoat I had sewn maybe another four or five inches to give me a little more protection. And the Captain again says, "Hey, what do you think, are we gonna stay out here all night or are we gonna go into town?" I said, "Let's go to town." He said, "Okay. Go ahead."

So there I was again, up there up ahead. We had one pair of field glasses who -- the guy that had it was an artillery observer. You couldn't call in any artillery if you wanted to. Radery was with me and we started down the road. We spot about 80 guys coming 90 degrees to us from another road and we were up on this high ground on somewhat of a road footpath. I take the guy who was a scout, a guy by the name of Geribeck [ph]. Geribeck. Not Jurasik. Geribeck. Two different guys.

We get up on the hill. The road was this way and the road was also going like so and there was a Volkswagen at the bottom of that hill, too, and these 80 guys were coming this way walking up the road just pretty as you please. Geribeck and I got on the hill. I got Radery gonna fire straight up the road and the rest of the company, the two guys we had, was on the other side of the hill. So you had 'em like this. Murder. Then we unloaded on them and then Geribeck and I started back down. We started back down and there was a little footpath there that had been worn and, again, this Volkswagen was here. Pretty soon bullets were coming at us and ole Geribeck hit the ground and I hit the ground right behind him.

You make a move like this, I'll make a countermove. You're not only nervous, you've got cat-like reflexes, I'll tell ya. So he hit the ground, I hit the ground behind him in this little gully and my head was -- his feet were here, my head was here stretched out on the ground and I kept looking to see where the hell is this stuff coming from. And the bullets were tracing my body like this, coming in between his feet and my head. I said, "For Christ sake, we can't stay here." So I told ole Geribeck "Get your ass up. Let's go." Well, about that time he said he was shot, and I finally realized it had to be coming from our guys and I stood up there and yelled and screamed and -- those trigger-happy devils, it's a wonder they didn't plug me then, too. And the Captain, Patterson, was down there and he started yelling at these guys and it was our guys that were killing us -- or killed him. And all of that commotion, we finally stopped. We left these guys up at the road there, we didn't give a shit what happened to them. I mean, the Germans, we didn't give a damn.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Steve A. Kallas
sp.p: And we picked him up. He was spitting beautiful lung tissue about chunks like that. So he was - he was full of lead. So we made a makeshift litter, carried him into town, and that's where these guys were gonna be as a welcoming committee for us, but we got 'em before they got to town. So that was the day - that was the day I was gonna get shot from the previous night's dream. Well, anyway, son of bitch. So we got into town and we didn't have any medics, no way to get back, and the guy said he wanted to take a crap. Pardon the expression. He had a bowel movement. And I searched the house trying to find a thunder mug or something to sit underneath him. We sat him up in bed. And of course what it had to be was the blood getting down to the lower portion of his body and feeling the pressure of a bowel movement. He didn't survive; he bled to death.

And I contacted his family after I got the computer, the Internet and so on -- now, this was several years ago -- and all his family had -- he just had some distant relatives that knew who he was and that was about it. But I wrote them a letter. And Wadsworth, the same way. So anyway, it was coming down to the short strokes of the war and we had to cross the Danube River, which I recall looking at it, it looked pretty blue to me.

You know, we had - we had to get around -- the whole regiment was supposed to go across that river to Salzburg and we had rubber boats. They got us some rubber boats and we all jumped in the rubber boats. Not one; a whole bunch of 'em. And start paddling like hell to get to the other side. And of course you had a welcoming committee on the other side. But of the three regiments, which 394th, there was 395th, and the 393rd. 393, 394, 395th. The 395th got about wiped out getting across the river there, but luckily we didn't. We had very small fire. We just paddled quick enough that we got across. So we got into town there -- and there again, the story of this thing -- got into the house.

There was feeble old ladies in there and I wasn't about to kick them out. Poor old - poor old, skinny old ladies. And there was tanks running up and down the street there blowing up things and so it wasn't a safe place to kick them out and I wasn't about to do that. Here we were, we got the squad in there, six or eight guys. We had some guys that were raw, raw, raw recruits. I mean, didn't know shit. Well, anyway, I was leaning inside the house against the door frame about like this, but it would be a door frame, you know, and the other guys were cleaning their rifles sitting on some nice furniture and this one asshole didn't realize that his chamber wasn't empty.

He lets one go and it just missed my head again, whoop. And I felt bad for the old ladies because they about shook themselves to pieces, they were so frightened. And of course I had to go back there and calm them down and -- but this idiot could have killed me. And he was a young guy out of New York, one of those New York types, and he could have killed me again and after -- this was toward the end of the war. A short while after that we were -- it was really grinding down to the end and when the armistice came -- or a cease-fire, we were still out in the woods and our first inkling was that the war was over, but we heard a lot of shooting. We didn't know that was it.

But there again, the first thing you do is you hit the ground and wonder what's goin' on and found out it was no more shooting. The next day or so we had some memorial services, which was, you know, the 21 shots in the air and blowing Taps and that was the end of it and then we got some barrack duty in -- near Munich to guard SS troops. We were guarding SS troops. Those were the rottenest sons of bitches on earth. They were mean devils and, you know... but they weren't so mean in the compound.

We used to take 'em out in the morning. One NCO and three other guys would be in charge of 50 guys going into Munich to bust rock, to clean up the destruction that was there. You know, make it easier for the civilians, right? One day one guy -- one of the German prisoners, the SS, snuck off. He must have been living in that town so he knew where he was going. Somebody made a comment "If he doesn't show up, we're gonna shoot you son of a bitches." We wouldn't have done that, but they believed it because they had done it. Well, anyway, when the guy came back, they grabbed him, one guy in each arm, one on each leg, and beat the living hell out of him with their shovels. They beat him to a bloody pulp and then threw him on the truck and that was the end of that guy.

And when those fellas would fall out for work in the morning, they would fall out in formation, march out, get on their trucks. They'd have bread and coffee for breakfast, soup and bread for supper -- or soup and bread, that's it. When they would come back in, they'd fall in. They'd start parade formation, man. Whoop, whoop, whoop, in. At night they would be in parade formation, very, very military like and after working hard all day and not eating too much. But the thing was that the -- there was a ration dump on the other side of the barbed wire and those devils tunneled out underneath that barbed wire, got over to the ration dump and they got rations inside. So somebody may have been eating pretty good. But we were also pilfering the ration dump because we weren't getting rations worth a damn either. I guess they must have figured -- I don't understand why they treated the infantry so badly. I know why.

Because they figured the mentality -- we were college guys, they put us in with these other fellas. I'm not disparaging. Those guys -- some of those guys were good soldiers, but not too swift in the way of mentality, and I'm not bragging. I probably had one of the highest IQs of the whole friggin' bunch. Officers, all they needed was 110 to get into OCS. I probably had a 140 IQ.

I used to yell and scream in the middle of the night and not even know it. I'd wake up and, you know, you don't know what the hell's going on. She would tell me about it once in a while. But this went on for at least 20 years, rising up in bed yelling and screaming "Whoa Nelly!" I mean - I mean, you would hear everything that was going on. Machine gunfire, mortars, artillery, you name it. And, again, I didn't even know it the next day, but I was awfully tired. Oh God almighty.
[THIS IS THE END OF DISK TWO]
